content: Stomatitis refers to the inflammation of the mucosal lining within the oral cavity, which can affect areas such as the cheeks, gums, tongue, lips, throat, and the roof or floor of the mouth. This condition may arise due to local factors, such as poor oral hygiene, ill-fitting dentures, or thermal injuries from hot food or beverages. It can also result from systemic conditions, including medication side effects, allergic reactions, or infections. A specific type of stomatitis, known as stomatitis nicotina, is caused by smoking cigars, cigarettes, or pipes and is characterized by small red bumps on the roof of the mouth. When the inflammation extends to the gingiva, it is referred to as gingivostomatitis. Irritation and cracking at the corners of the lips are termed angular stomatitis or angular cheilitis. There is no universally accepted classification system for stomatitis. However, it can be categorized based on its etiology or the pathogens involved. Stomatitis can be infectious or non-infectious in nature. Infectious causes include bacterial, viral, and fungal origins, such as necrotizing ulcerative stomatitis (noma), herpetic gingivostomatitis, Vincent’s stomatitis (trench mouth), and candidal stomatitis. Non-infectious causes include autoimmune conditions like aphthous stomatitis, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), pemphigus vulgaris, bullous pemphigoid, Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), and pyostomatitis vegetans. Drug-induced stomatitis can result from chemotherapy, antibiotics, antihistamines, monoclonal antibodies, or antirheumatic agents. Irritant-induced stomatitis may occur due to poorly maintained dentures, contact allergens, or smoking (stomatitis nicotina). Other causes include tumors, black hairy tongue, burning mouth syndrome, migratory stomatitis (geographic stomatitis), and chronic ulcerative stomatitis. The pathophysiology of stomatitis involves inflammation of the oral mucosa, with mechanisms varying depending on the type. For example, the exact pathogenesis of aphthous stomatitis is unknown but is thought to involve immune system abnormalities, autoimmune antibodies, and cytokine or T-cell accumulation, leading to defective cell-mediated immunity. Recurrence is common in aphthous ulcers. Stomatitis can be caused by various factors, including herpes virus infections, poor oral hygiene, and nutritional deficiencies. The epidemiology and demographics differ among types. Herpetic gingivostomatitis is most common in children aged 6 months to 5 years, while noma primarily affects children, and pyostomatitis vegetans is more common in individuals aged 20 to 50 years. Risk factors for stomatitis include smoking, alcohol consumption, trauma, psychological stress, nutritional deficiencies, and immunocompromised states. Preventive measures, such as routine screening, are not currently recommended due to insufficient evidence. If untreated, herpetic stomatitis typically resolves after vesicles rupture and ulcers heal. The herpes simplex virus (HSV) remains latent in ganglia and can reactivate under immunocompromised conditions, causing recurrent oral vesicles. Viral shedding may persist for 2–12 days after the primary infection. Complications of stomatitis include meningoencephalitis, recurrent skin and oral infections, dissemination of infection, and tooth loss. The prognosis is generally favorable. Diagnosis of stomatitis relies on a thorough history and clinical examination. Key findings include the location and characteristics of ulcers, as well as symptoms such as fever, anorexia, irritability, drooling, malaise, and headache. Physical examination may reveal oral vesicles, mucosal ulcers, submandibular lymphadenitis, and halitosis. Laboratory tests, such as viral cultures, Tzanck smears, serology, immunofluorescence studies, and PCR, can aid in diagnosing herpetic stomatitis. Imaging techniques like X-rays, CT, MRI, and ultrasound are not typically useful for stomatitis. Treatment focuses on preventive measures and medical therapy. Key principles include maintaining hydration (oral or IV), pain control, and the application of barrier creams or gels, such as Zilactin (a combination of lidocaine and hydroxypropyl cellulose) to prevent trauma and irritation. Surgical intervention is generally not recommended unless there is suspicion of an oral tumor or a biopsy is needed. Surgical debridement may be necessary for conditions like noma or trench mouth. Primary prevention strategies include adequate hydration, oral hygiene, denture hygiene, and avoiding exposure to bovine papular stomatitis virus-infected cattle. Secondary prevention involves managing underlying conditions, such as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), to prevent associated complications like pyostomatitis vegetans.
